title: Contest Toolkit: Number Theory & Range Queries
caps: O of n log log n

scenes.say: Contest answers are too big. Compute three to the thirteen mod seven in five multiplications. By the end you'll do both. Then answer range sums while values change, in log n.

lines.text: Range sums while values change, in log n

scenes.say: Today you will do three things. Do arithmetic mod a big prime, with fast powers and gcd. List primes with a sieve. And answer range queries with a Fenwick tree or a segment tree.

scenes.title: Ten o'clock plus five hours
scenes.statement: A twelve-hour clock wraps around. Find the hour five hours after ten o'clock.
scenes.say: Ten o'clock, and five hours pass. What hour does the clock show? Three o'clock.

scenes.head: Mod is clock arithmetic
scenes.say: A clock wraps at twelve. It's ten o'clock. Add five hours: fifteen, which wraps to three o'clock. That wrap is mod. In contests we mod by one billion seven. The remainder always fits.

scenes.head: Mod rules, gcd and lcm
scenes.say: The constant is one billion seven, a prime. Reduce mod after every add and multiply. Both inputs below it, so a product fits in sixty four bits. Subtraction needs the plus M fix. Gcd, the greatest common divisor, is a library call. Lcm, the least common multiple, divides first so it can't overflow.
Warm-up. In C plus plus, what does three minus five, then percent seven, print? Lock in a guess.

scenes.head: Negative remainders
scenes.say: Negative two. C plus plus keeps the sign of the left side, so the remainder can be negative. Add seven and take mod again: five, the true clock answer. That's why subtraction needs plus M.

scenes.head: Euclid: gcd(48, 18)
scenes.say: How does gcd work? Replace the pair with the second number and the remainder. Forty eight mod eighteen is twelve. Eighteen mod twelve is six. Twelve mod six is zero. When the remainder is zero, that's the answer: six. So huge answers stay small.

scenes.title: Huge answer, small remainder
scenes.statement: Contest answers are astronomically large. Print them modulo 1,000,000,007.
scenes.say: Imagine a thirty one digit answer. Contests want its remainder mod one billion seven. Fast power gets two to the hundredth: nine seven six, three seven one, two eight five.

scenes.title: Fast power
scenes.statement: Compute a big power modulo m without multiplying e times.
scenes.say: Three to the thirteenth, mod seven. The slow way takes twelve multiplications. The fast way takes five, and gives three.

scenes.head: 13 in binary: 1101
scenes.say: Thirteen in binary is one one zero one: eight plus four plus one. So three to the thirteen is three to the eight, times three to the four, times three to the one. Squaring builds each power. Four squarings, the last one unused. Two real multiplies, so five that matter. The first bit just sets it.

scenes.head: 3^13 mod 7, step by step
scenes.say: Start: result one, base three, exponent thirteen. Odd, so result becomes three. Square the base: two. Halve the exponent: six. Even: square the base, four, exponent three. Odd: result three times four, mod seven, is five. Square: two, exponent one. Odd: result five times two is three. Done: three.

scenes.head: Fast power in code
scenes.say: The loop in code. If the lowest bit of e is set, multiply the result. Always square the base, and shift e right. That's O of log e multiplications, not e. It prints three, then two to the hundredth mod one billion seven.

Try this one. Fermat says the inverse of a is a to the p minus two, because a to the p minus one is one mod p. Fermat needs a prime modulus. Otherwise use extended Euclid: a gcd that also returns x and y, where a times x plus m times y equals the gcd. What is the inverse of three mod seven? Commit to a number.

scenes.head: Inverse of 3 mod 7
scenes.say: Five. Three to the fifth is two forty three, which is five mod seven. And three times five is fifteen, which is one mod seven. So dividing by three means multiplying by five.

scenes.head: Three modular traps
scenes.say: Three traps. Fermat's inverse needs a prime modulus. Otherwise use extended Euclid. Multiply three numbers and the product overflows before the mod: reduce after every times. And plain power loops e times, too slow.
rows: needs a prime m; else extended Euclid
power by a loop of e

scenes.title: All primes up to 30
scenes.statement: List every prime up to n, fast.
scenes.say: Which numbers up to thirty are prime? Ten of them, two up to twenty nine. And n might be ten million.

scenes.head: Sieve of Eratosthenes, up to 30
scenes.say: Write the numbers one to thirty. One isn't prime, so it's out. Cross out the multiples of two, starting at four. Next survivor, three: cross out its multiples, starting at nine. Next, five: its first new multiple is twenty five. Seven squared is forty nine, past thirty, so stop. Everything left standing is prime.

scenes.head: Sieve in code
scenes.say: Assume everything is prime, except zero and one. For each surviving i, start crossing at i squared, since smaller multiples were crossed by smaller primes. Stop when i squared passes n. Count the survivors: ten. Time is O of n log log n, nearly linear.
Quick check. Sieve up to one hundred. Which prime is the last whose multiples get crossed out? Say your answer out loud.
scenes.q: Sieve up to 100: last prime crossed out?

scenes.head: Where the sieve stops at 100
scenes.say: Seven. Two squared is four, three squared nine, five squared twenty five, seven squared forty nine. Eleven squared is one twenty one, past one hundred, so we stop.

scenes.head: Sieve follow-ups
scenes.say: Sieve time is n log log n. To test one number, trial division up to its square root is enough. And i times i is fine as an int here.
rows: O(n log log n), nearly linear
fine for n up to 10^7; overflows only past about 2 billion

scenes.title: Range sums with updates
scenes.statement: Answer sums of a prefix while single values change.

example.input: [5, 2, 9, 1, 7]: sum of first 4, add 3 at index 2, sum again

scenes.say: Five, two, nine, one, seven. Sum the first four. Add three at index two. Sum again. Seventeen, then twenty. Now imagine two hundred thousand of those.

scenes.head: Cost of each idea, n values
scenes.say: This table measures steps per operation. A plain array updates in one step, but a sum scans n. Prefix sums answer in one step, but an update rewrites up to n. A Fenwick tree does both in log n.

scenes.head: Fenwick: subtotals, then a sum
scenes.say: Here are five values. The tree stores subtotals. T one holds the first value, five. T three holds nine, and t five holds seven. T two covers two values: seven. T four covers four: seventeen. The sum of the first four is just t four: seventeen. One step, not four.

scenes.head: Fenwick: add 3 at index 2
scenes.say: Now add three at index two. Which subtotals contain index two? T two, then t four. Add three to each: ten, then twenty. The sum of the first four is now twenty.

scenes.head: Query goes down
scenes.say: Query goes down: subtract the lowest bit each time, adding subtotals. Lowbit is the value of the lowest one bit. Lowbit of six is two. A range sum is sum of r minus sum of l minus one.

scenes.head: Update goes up
scenes.say: Update goes up: add the lowest bit each time, fixing every subtotal that covers i. Both loops run at most log n times.
Now you try. After the update the array is five, five, nine, one, seven. What is the sum of the first three? Name it before I do.
scenes.q: After the update, sum of the first 3 values?

scenes.head: sum(3) after the update
scenes.say: Nineteen. Start at i equals three: add t three, nine. Drop the lowest bit: i is two. Add t two, now ten. Drop again: i is zero, stop. Nine plus ten is nineteen.

scenes.head: Run it: 17, then 20
scenes.say: Load the values with add, one at a time. Sum of the first four prints seventeen. Add three at index two. Sum again: twenty.

scenes.head: Fenwick traps
scenes.say: Index zero is the classic bug: the loop never moves. Fenwick needs an operation you can subtract, like sums. For min or max, use a segment tree.
rows: can't subtract: use a segment tree

scenes.title: Range minimum with updates
scenes.statement: Find the smallest value in a half-open range [l, r) while values change.
scenes.say: Five, two, nine, one. Half open means start included, end excluded. Smallest from one to four? One. And the values can change.

scenes.head: A knockout tournament
scenes.say: Think of a knockout tournament where each match keeps the smaller score. Four players, two matches, one final. The winner of everything sits at the top. That's a segment tree: every parent stores the combination of its two children.

scenes.head: Segment tree for min
scenes.say: Leaves hold the array: five, two, nine, one. Each parent holds the smaller of its children. Two, and one. The root holds the smallest of everything: one. Swap min for plus and the same tree stores sums.

scenes.head: Query: take whole blocks
scenes.say: Min over the half open range, one to four, four excluded. Take the leaf holding two. Then the block above nine and one, which already holds one. Min of two and one: one. Two pieces, not three leaves.

scenes.head: Update: walk up the parents
scenes.say: To update, set the leaf, then walk up. At each step the parent becomes the min of its two children. One step per level, so O of log n. Setting position one to eight leaves the root at one, and the parent at five.

scenes.head: Query in code
scenes.say: Half open: l is in, r is out. Start at both leaves and walk inward. If l is odd, take it and step right. If r is odd, step left and take it. Only whole blocks: O of log n.
Last check. After setting position one to eight, what is the min over the range zero up to, not including, two? Hold your guess.

scenes.head: After the update: min(5, 8) = 5
scenes.say: Five. The leaf became eight, and its parent is the smaller of five and eight. Two would be stale. The root still holds one, from the nine and one block.

scenes.head: Segment tree vs Fenwick
scenes.say: Fenwick for sums, short code. Segment tree for min and max. Range updates? Lazy propagation keeps pending updates, pushed down when needed. Query range? Half open: start included, end excluded. Build time? Fenwick, n adds, O of n log n. Segment tree, O of n.
rows: Fenwick: sums, short. Segment tree: min, max, lazy
lazy propagation: pending updates pushed down
Fenwick: n adds, O(n log n); segment tree: O(n)

scenes.head: Say it in 20 seconds
scenes.say: Why mod one billion seven? Prime, and products fit in sixty four bits. Fast power? O of log e. Inverse? Fermat, prime modulus only. GCD? Euclid: the pair becomes the second number and the remainder, O of log n. Sieve time? n log log n. Mistake? Overflow before the mod.
rows: Euclid: gcd(a, b) = gcd(b, a mod b), O(log n)

scenes.head: Say it in 20 seconds
scenes.say: Range sums with updates? Fenwick or segment tree, O of log n each. Which one? Fenwick for sums, segment tree for min, max, lazy. Why lowbit? Cell i sums lowbit values ending at i, so steps jump whole blocks. Mistake? Fenwick is one indexed.
rows: Fenwick or segment tree: O(log n)
Fenwick: sums. Segment: min, max, lazy
cell i holds the sum of the lowbit(i) values ending at i, so each loop step jumps a whole block
index 0 in a Fenwick: infinite loop

scenes.head: Practice before your interview
scenes.say: Solve these three next. LeetCode two oh four, Count Primes, is the sieve. LeetCode fifty, Pow of x and n, is fast power. LeetCode three oh seven, Range Sum Query Mutable, is a Fenwick tree.
So say this. Reduce mod after every step. Fast power takes log e multiplications. A sieve lists primes in n log log n. Fenwick and segment trees take log n.
lines: Fast power: O(log e). Sieve: O(n log log n).
Fenwick or segment tree: O(log n).
